package_info.package_name: N/A (commit spoofing technique, not a specific package)
package_info.package_manager: N/A (applies to any Git-based workflow, including GitHub)
package_info.why_malicious: This technique is malicious because it enables attackers to falsify the historical record of code contributions by manipulating commit timestamps in Git repositories. By artificially creating a deceptive appearance of long-term, consistent, and active development, attackers can build fraudulent trust in malicious or fraudulent open-source projects and developer profiles, potentially deceiving users, maintainers, and automated trust systems.

execution_context.trigger: pre-commit (manual or scripted execution before git commit or push)
execution_context.file_location: executed in terminal or within automation scripts in the local git repository environment
required_permissions: environment_vars (ability to set GIT_AUTHOR_DATE and GIT_COMMITTER_DATE)
filesystem (write access to local git repository)

malicious_snippets.code_snippet:
set git GIT_AUTHOR_DATE=2010-04-19 17:18:43
set git GIT_COMMITTER_DATE=2010-04-19 17:18:43
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: Before committing, the code sets the GIT_AUTHOR_DATE and GIT_COMMITTER_DATE environment variables to arbitrary past values, which alters the metadata of subsequent git commits so that they appear to have been made at those times, resulting in a falsified commit history and misleading activity graph.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: This behavior is suspicious because it deliberately manipulates the commit metadata to misrepresent the timing and authenticity of code contributions, undermining the integrity of the repository's history and potentially deceiving users and automated systems that rely on commit timelines for trust assessment.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal git workflows expect commit timestamps to accurately reflect when code changes were made. In this case, the timestamps are intentionally falsified to create a misleading narrative of project activity and developer involvement.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Legitimate use cases for setting commit dates include correcting timezone errors, importing legacy code with accurate historical dates, or preserving original authorship during repository migration. However, systematic or large-scale manipulation of commit dates, especially to predate repository or user creation, is highly atypical and indicative of malicious intent.
key_indicators: Commits with author or committer dates that predate the repository or user account creation date
Large numbers of commits with identical or sequentially manipulated timestamps
Commit activity patterns that are inconsistent with normal development (e.g., hundreds of commits in a short period, or regular intervals over years)
Discrepancies between commit dates and other repository metadata (e.g., first commit predates repo creation)

attack_chain.action: Attacker sets GIT_AUTHOR_DATE and GIT_COMMITTER_DATE environment variables to arbitrary past dates before making commits.
attack_chain.leads_to: Commits are created with falsified timestamps, embedding manipulated dates in the git history.

attack_chain.action: Attacker pushes these manipulated commits to a remote repository (e.g., GitHub), populating the activity graph and commit history with fake activity.
attack_chain.leads_to: The repository and associated developer profile appear to have a long history of legitimate development activity, increasing perceived trust and credibility.

behavioral_signatures: Commits with author or committer dates that predate the repository or user account creation date
Unusual density or regularity in commit timestamps (e.g., hundreds of commits in a short time, or perfectly regular intervals over long periods)
Bulk commits with identical or near-identical timestamps
Commit history patterns inconsistent with typical development workflows
file_indicators: No direct file indicators; detection requires analysis of git commit metadata and repository history
network_indicators: No direct network indicators; suspicious activity is observable via repository metadata through the GitHub API or web interface
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Automate analysis of git commit metadata to identify inconsistencies, such as commit dates before repository or user creation, unnatural commit frequency or patterns, and bulk commits with identical or sequentially manipulated timestamps. Use the GitHub API to cross-reference commit dates with repository and user creation dates. Flag repositories or accounts exhibiting these anomalies for further manual review or automated trust scoring adjustment.
